name: Interview behavioural questions, set 1
description: Spoken behavioural questions with model answers and rubrics: a mistake, a disagreement, why trading, a project, a decision. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a time you got something wrong, at work or at university. What changed afterwards?
widget.model: In my second year I ran the data work for a four-person project on bus delays. We had a week to model a year of timetable data. My job was the cleaning and the first model. I dropped every row with a missing arrival time without asking why it was missing. Our model said delays fell 20% in winter, which looked odd. A teammate asked why. I went back and found the missing rows were mostly cancelled winter services. I had thrown away the worst delays. I told the group that evening and owned the mistake. I redid the cleaning with cancellations counted as long delays and reran the model. The winter effect flipped to a 15% rise. That matched the operator's own published report. We submitted on time and got the top mark in our seminar group. Since then I write down why data is missing before I drop anything. I also check one surprising result by hand before I trust it.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: one clear mistake that you made yourself
A specific situation: when, what the task was, and what was at stake
Your own actions named in the first person, including owning the mistake
A number or concrete result, before and after the fix
A habit you changed, stated plainly
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer names one mistake that was yours, what you did about it, and what you do differently now. Keep the situation short and spend most of the time on your actions. Avoid a "weakness" that is really a strength.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Describe a disagreement with a teammate. How did you settle it?
widget.model: Last year I was in a team of three in a society trading competition. Each team ran a strategy on a simulated market for four weeks. A week in, my teammate wanted to replace our simple trend rule with a neural network he had built. I thought it was overfitted. We argued for two evenings and got nowhere. So I suggested a test we would both accept before seeing the result. We held back the last month of the practice data, which neither model had seen. Whichever had the better risk-adjusted return there would run. I wrote the test harness and he wrote the comparison report, so neither of us marked our own work. His model lost 4% on the held-back month, while the trend rule made 2%. He agreed to keep the rule and to use his model only to size trades. We finished second of eighteen teams. I learned to turn an argument about opinions into a test agreed in advance.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: who disagreed, and about what
A specific situation with a real stake, not a clash of personalities
Your own actions to settle it, in the first person, fair to the other view
A number or concrete outcome of how it was settled
What you learned about settling disagreements
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer keeps the disagreement about the work and shows how it was settled fairly. Agreeing a test before seeing the result is a good method. Never make the other person the villain.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Why do you want to trade, rather than work in research or on a bank's desk?
widget.model: I want to trade because I like making decisions under uncertainty and getting a fast, honest answer from a price. A trader at a market maker quotes, takes risk and adjusts many times a day. Research suits people who want months on one question. I enjoy research, but I work best with quicker feedback. A bank desk is closer, but much of the work there serves clients. I want my own risk and my own decisions. My evidence is a university trading society game I played for a term. I made markets in card and dice contracts against twenty players. I finished first twice, and I kept a log of every losing trade. Reviewing that log each week was the part I liked most. So I want a firm that trains traders on its own capital, with a lot of practice and review.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence with a reason, not "I like markets"
Shows what the trading job involves day to day
Contrasts fairly with research and with a bank desk
Evidence from your own experience, with a number
Links the reasons to this kind of firm
Under two minutes, clear, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer says what the trading job is and why it suits you, with evidence. Contrast the other roles fairly, without running them down. Close by linking your reasons to the kind of firm in front of you.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Walk me through a project you owned: the goal, the decisions you made and the result.
widget.model: Last summer I built a backtest of a pairs-trading rule on ten years of daily prices for forty UK shares. The goal was to find out whether a rule from a textbook still made money after costs. First, I held back the last two years before looking at any results. That way I could not tune on them. Second, I charged 5 basis points a trade, which I took from published spreads. I rejected minute data: it was costly to get, and daily data answered the question. Before costs the rule had a Sharpe ratio of 1.3 on the training years. After costs it fell to 0.4. On the two held-back years it was 0.1, so I concluded the edge had mostly gone. I wrote it up in six pages and put the code on a public repository. If I did it again, I would test the cost assumption first, since it changed the answer most.

rubric.text: States the goal in one sentence, and why it mattered
Two or more decisions you made, each with its reason
One alternative you rejected and the trade-off behind it
Numbers for the result, including any that disappointed
What you would do differently
Within three minutes, ordered goal, decisions, result

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong account names the goal, the decisions you made and why, and an honest result with numbers. A disappointing result told clearly is better than a vague success. End with what you would change.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: You must choose between two options, and you have about half the information you would like. Talk me through how you decide.
widget.model: Let me make it concrete. Say I must put £10,000 behind one of two strategies, with six months of results instead of a year. First, the goal: the better return for the risk, without a large loss. What I know: strategy A made 6% with small swings, and B made 9% with one 12% drawdown. What is missing: how each behaves in a sell-off, and six months is too short to tell skill from luck. That gap matters most, because a large loss is the outcome I most want to avoid. Next, is the choice reversible? If I can move the money monthly, a wrong choice costs little. So I would decide now: A gets £7,000 and B gets £3,000, sized by the downside. I would review in three months. If B shows no drawdown over 12% then, I would move more into it. If A starts losing in a falling market, I would cut it.

rubric.text: Restates the decision and the goal before choosing
Separates what is known from what is missing, and says which gap matters most
Puts rough numbers on the outcomes or the downside
Makes a decision and says it aloud, not only a process
Names the new information that would change the choice
Thinks aloud in order, without long silences

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Interviewers want the structure: the goal, what you know, what is missing, and the cost of each mistake. Then decide, and say what would change your mind. A process with no decision at the end misses the point.
